meta.title: The Night FedEx Went to Vegas
meta.subtitle: What really saved FedEx, and three rules every founder can use
meta.audience: aspiring founders and curious viewers; no business background needed
meta.disclaimer: Educational storytelling. Disputed and attributed details are labelled. Not business or financial advice.
learning_goals: Explain why a startup with a good idea can still die: cash, not the idea, sets the deadline
Tell the difference between buying time and building a business
Recognise network ideas that only work at full size, and why they need long funding

principles.name: Cash is oxygen
principles.line: A startup doesn't die when its idea is bad. It dies when the money runs out.

beats.narration: FedEx had about five thousand dollars left. Then its founder flew to Las Vegas.
It sounds like the greatest comeback in business. It's also the most misunderstood. In the next four minutes, you'll see what really saved FedEx, and three rules every founder can use.

visual.title: The Night FedEx Went to Vegas

beats.narration: We love the legend of the founder who bets everything and wins. One brilliant idea, one bold move, and the rest is history. This story says otherwise.

visual.caption: Bet it all. Win it all?

beats.narration: Fred Smith was a former Marine officer who served two tours in Vietnam. In nineteen seventy one he founded Federal Express, putting in about four million dollars of his own inheritance.

visual.name: Fred Smith
visual.role: Marine officer · Founder of Federal Express

beats.narration: You may have heard he first described the idea in a Yale paper, and got a C. The paper was real. The C is legend. Asked years later, Smith said he didn't know his grade. He had probably made his usual C.

left.title: The legend
items: His professor gave the idea a C
Retold in business books for decades

right.title: The record
items: Smith: he didn't know his grade

beats.narration: His idea was simple, and a little strange. Fly every package to one city, Memphis, in the middle of the night. Sort it. Then fly it out again before morning. Even a package going next door would travel through Memphis.
On April seventeenth, nineteen seventy three, fourteen small jets took off to serve twenty five cities. That first night, they carried one hundred and eighty six packages.
And the money started burning. The planes flew every night, full or not. Fuel kept getting more expensive. Within about two years, the company had lost close to thirty million dollars.

Then came the week the story is famous for. By one account, FedEx had about five thousand dollars in the bank, and a fuel bill of some twenty four thousand due on Monday. Smith asked the conglomerate General Dynamics for more money. They said no.

So, as founding executive Roger Frock tells it, Smith reportedly took the last five thousand dollars to Las Vegas, played blackjack, and won about twenty seven thousand. Enough to pay for the fuel. The planes kept flying.

visual.kicker: Las Vegas · as the story goes
visual.caption: $5,000 became $32,000

beats.narration: Here's the part the legend skips. Twenty seven thousand dollars bought FedEx about one more week. The company was losing far more than that. Even Smith reportedly called the win not decisive. Just an omen.

visual.text: The $27,000 wasn't decisive, but it was an omen that things would get better.

beats.narration: What really saved FedEx was slower, and far less exciting. Smith kept pitching investors, again and again, and raised tens of millions of dollars more, enough to keep the network flying until the planes filled up. In nineteen seventy six, FedEx made its first profit, about three point six million dollars.

Lesson one. Cash is oxygen. FedEx's idea was right, and it still almost died. A company doesn't die when its idea is bad. It dies when the money runs out. So always know how many weeks of cash you have left.
Lesson two. A gamble buys time, not a business. The blackjack win bought one week. Investors who believed in the plan bought years. Take luck when it comes, but never make it your plan.

visual.caption: A gamble buys time, not a business

beats.narration: Lesson three. Some ideas only work at full size. One plane to Memphis is useless. Twenty five cities connected every night is a network. Half a network is worth almost nothing, so FedEx had to survive the expensive years while it grew.

visual.caption: Some ideas only work at full size

beats.narration: Now test yourself. Your startup has three weeks of cash, and your biggest customer just said maybe. Which move actually saves you?

visual.question: Three weeks of cash. Your biggest customer said maybe. Which move saves you?
choices: One big bet to win cash fast
Cut costs and raise money from people who believe in the plan
visual.answer: Cut costs and raise money. A gamble buys time, not a business.

beats.narration: So, three lessons from the night FedEx went to Vegas. Cash is oxygen. A gamble buys time, not a business. And some ideas only work at full size.

items.text: A gamble buys time, not a business

beats.narration: Fred Smith did go to Las Vegas. But a lucky night is not why FedEx flies today. The bet made the legend. Surviving made the company.

visual.caption: The bet made the legend. Surviving made the company.
